newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Hun Sen troops force opposition retreat in north.
newsitem.headline: Hun Sen troops force opposition retreat in north.

text.p: Backed by tanks and artillery, forces loyal to Second Prime Minister Hun Sen advanced west along Cambodia's Highway Six about 40 km (25 miles) west of the city of Siem Reap on Saturday, forcing opposition troops to retreat.
The two sides exchanged artillery, rocket, mortar, machine-gun and small-arms fire, but kept their distance from each other on a flat plain dominated by rice paddies and occasional clusters of trees.

A steady stream of civilians from small villages in the area, including Sor Sadam and nearby Plang, fled the fighting on foot and by motorbike, pausing occasionally under shady trees along the road to peer back anxiously in the direction of their homes.

"I heard the sound of fighting this morning at six a.m. It was very heavy and very near," said Noung Saming, 47, a farmer from Plang district escaping on a motorcycle with his wife, son, and two bags of rice.

"I returned to my village in 1979 after the Pol Pot time and this is the first time I have had to leave," he told Reuters. "I am worried because I left some belongings behind and I'm afraid they may be stolen."
Reporters saw two bridges which had been destroyed. Highway Six, the main link betwen Siem Reap and the Thai border to the west is now impassable to all motor vehicles.
One wooden bridge was blown up on Friday by government troops to prevent opposition forces advancing towards Siem Reap, which is close to the temples of Angkor, Cambodia's main tourist attraction.
Residents said the other, larger, concrete-and-steel bridge was blown up by retreating opposition forces last Sunday.

The residents referred to the retreating soldiers as Khmer Rouge guerrillas but observers said it was likely they included soldiers loyal to First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, who was ousted by Hun Sen's forces after two days of fighting in Phnom Penh last weekend.

The government advance on Saturday brought to mind countless images of past wars in Indochina with two tanks clanking down the red-dirt highway, flanked by infantry standing up in rice paddies on either side.
A dozen soldiers walked ahead of the lead tank scouring the road for mines, using only their eyes and a single hand-held mine detector.
A number of anti-personnel mines and a single anti-tank mine were uncovered along the route.
The soldiers touted ancient Soviet-style Kalashnikov assault rifles and more modern American-made M-16s as they moved west wearing flip-flops and red-checked kramas, the ubiquitous Cambodian scarf.
The tanks were strapped with extra fuel, metal ammunition containers, sacks of rice, grey cans of water and trussed-up chickens blinking in the blinding sun.
A government multiple-barreled rocket launcher fired several rockets without warning shortly after noon, launching the projectiles with a deafening shriek on columns of flame.
An hour later two government tanks and a number of trucks loaded with soldiers rushed down the highway west of Siem Reap towards the retreating opposition forces.
Reporters saw six government tanks, three armoured personnel carriers and two multiple-barreled rocket launchers, known as "Stalin organs" on the government side of the line.
Saturday's fighting never verged on full-pitched battle. Both sides seemed content to avoid close contact.
No government casualties were observed although one seriously ill soldier, perhaps suffering from malaria, was carried in a hammock back from the front line.
Chey Sem, 48, a village soldier in Prey Chouk, east of Saturday's fighting, said he was ready to evacuate his family if the opposition forces advanced.
Standing barefoot and shirtless on the highway, his chest elaborately tattoed, he shook his head when asked about the future.
"I am ready to fight if I have to. I'm ready to run away with my family if I have to. The important thing is not to be killed," he said.
